title: Kurigram's shrinking rivers cut off 550,000 char people
excerpt: Sandbars in 16 Kurigram rivers have doubled boat journeys and pushed nearly 100 ghats towards closure, UNB reports. The Water Development Board has no plan to dredge.

image.alt: A boat on the Brahmaputra River in Kurigram, Bangladesh
image.credit: Tanvir Rahat / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0

content:
Falling water and new sandbars in 16 rivers in Kurigram have left about 550,000 people in the district's char (river island) areas struggling to reach essential services, the news agency UNB reported on Thursday (26 November).

The Brahmaputra, Dharla, Teesta, Dudhkumar, Gangadhar and Sankosh rivers have become hard to navigate, UNB said. Boats take longer routes or get stuck in shallow stretches, and passengers often walk long distances across sandy riverbeds to reach landing points. Moving goods and emergency patients has become harder.

Jatrapur ghat in Kurigram Sadar upazila, which links to at least 50 other ghats, has shifted almost a kilometre because of sandbars, and the number of boats operating from it each day has fallen from more than 500 to about half that, according to the report. Journeys from Jatrapur to several chars now take almost twice as long. Boat owner Abdus Salam told UNB a trip to Doi Khowar Char in Ulipur upazila that used to take 45 minutes now takes about two and a half hours.

Nearly 100 river ghats are close to shutting, leaving thousands of boatmen and fishermen without regular work, UNB reported. Passengers said fares had risen by Tk 10 to Tk 20 because of sandbars and higher diesel prices, and hiring a boat in an emergency can cost Tk 1,500. Kurigram Water Development Board Executive Engineer Md Rakibul Hasan said there was no current plan to dredge the rivers, though a future project on the Brahmaputra-Jamuna system might help.

Why it matters

Kurigram is one of Bangladesh's poorest districts, and char households already face floods and erosion in the monsoon. In the dry season the same rivers isolate them in a different way: longer, costlier trips to clinics, schools, markets and government offices. Health, education and cash programmes in the chars need transport budgets and referral plans that account for this. Devlens has reported on how narrow bridges and culverts are choking rivers elsewhere.

What to watch

  • Whether the Water Development Board or BIWTA proposes dredging or emergency ghat works before the dry season peaks.
  • Any government-run boat service for char routes, which passengers asked for.
